anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 721 - PDF page 201 (word id 33024)
near_miss.lead: Hands and feet in bodily violence
near_miss.why_not: Armenian feet and hands are bound during torture. The epic elephant has a severed trunk (hasta) and feet; different predicates and referents defeat an inherited collocation. The Greek prayer uses raised hands, not binding.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 942 - PDF page 422 (word id 44843) (w1/2)
near_miss.why_not: The Armenian brings names into speech in the Joshua episode. Norse bera nafn means bear a title; Greek bears a man. No shared phrase with congruent syntax and sense.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 696 - PDF page 176 (word id 28744) (w1/2)
near_miss.lead: Glory given to a name in ritual address
near_miss.why_not: Explicit Psalm quotation in Armenian. Umbrian has invocation and a name but not the give-glory construction; second-person address alone is insufficient.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 762 - PDF page 242 (word id 39987) (w1/2)
near_miss.why_not: Both bare and foot/step material are cognate, but Armenian bok ew heti coordinates barefoot and on-foot, while Norse has an adjective modifying feet. The underlying condition is ordinary and the prayer versus military submission contexts do not establish a distinctive inherited formula. Corpus hits also show barefoot walking outside these contexts.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 695 - PDF page 175 (word id 28488)
near_miss.why_not: Armenian describes anxious sleeplessness, but the slab Herodotus passage concerns a vision appearing during sleep; its opsis is not eyes losing sleep. Closer Homeric search witnesses are recorded separately.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 951 - PDF page 431 (word id 48765) (w3/3)

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 947 - PDF page 427 (word id 47128) (w2/2)

search_lead.slab_anchor: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 695 - PDF page 175 (word id 28488)
search_lead.cognate: Armenian kʻown and Greek hypnos continue sleep *swep-; Armenian akn and Greek omma continue the eye root *h3ekw-.
search_lead.argument: The anxious magus loses sleep from his eyes; anxious Agamemnon cannot have sleep settle on his eyes, and watchmen have sleep gone from their eyelids. The latter substitutes eyelids. This is closer than the slab’s dream report, though a widespread physiological metaphor and biblical sleeplessness idioms must be controlled before inheritance is asserted.

search_lead.slab_anchor: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 645 - PDF page 125 (word id 20320)
search_lead.cognate: mec / mahat, great, and anown / nāman, name, are cognate.
search_lead.argument: Armenian gives Moses a great name after his act; Vedic applies great to the divine name. This supplies a genuine adjective/name pair absent from the bundle partners, but not the Armenian bestowal predicate. Generic greatness and biblical naming language remain serious alternative explanations.

search_lead.slab_anchor: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 938 - PDF page 418 (word id 42999) (w2/2)
search_lead.cognate: The number seven is inherited (Armenian eawtʻn, Sanskrit sapta); the full anatomical terms are not an exact cognate lexical set.
search_lead.argument: Armenian enumerates two eyes, ears and nostril channels plus mouth as seven fortifications in an allegory of Jericho. Atharvaveda enumerates the same seven head apertures, and elsewhere in the hymn has a nine-gated city. The differing numbers and lexical realization of the city figure, obvious anatomy, and Armenian biblical allegory preclude treating this as an established inherited formula; worth review as a figure-level lead.
